scenes.text: This is BrainSauce. It answers questions from the documents a company already keeps in Confluence, Jira, Slack, Drive and email, and every answer arrives with its evidence: which documents it used, how fresh each was, and what the asker was allowed to see.

John Tan runs finance operations and asks about the Rail-B cutover. The facts sit in an email, a Jira issue, two Slack channels and a vendor list. The answer brings them together as plain sentences, each ending in a citation, with a freshness receipt and an access summary underneath. The same question works over REST and from an MCP client.

Each question runs through one pipeline. Hybrid search over-fetches candidates. Access control removes what the asker may not read, before any model is called or any document text is loaded. Freshness checks the survivors, a sanitiser screens the text for prompt injection, one model call writes the answer, deterministic code verifies it, and the event joins a hash-chained audit log.

Permissions are stored in each platform's own shape, never flattened into one list. At query time a ten-rule policy evaluates every candidate for the asker in a fixed order, from explicit denies down to membership on the source platform, and the source platform sets the ceiling: a local grant cannot widen what Drive allows, and an administrator does not read everything. Anything unknown denies. A permission snapshot older than its classification permits, five minutes for confidential documents, denies too. A document you cannot read returns the same 404 as one that does not exist.

Mei Chen is an external contractor and asks for the Q3 board deck figures. The deck is confidential and Drive does not share it with Mei, so the answer abstains, and nothing confirms the deck exists. John asks the same question and gets the revenue figure, cited to the deck, which Drive shares with the leadership group. Now the Drive owner removes that group from the share. Nothing changes inside BrainSauce. The next sync reads the new permissions, John's next answer no longer uses the deck, and the earlier answer in John's history is withheld, because a saved answer is only as visible as its least visible evidence.

Every indexed object carries a freshness state, and policies set an age budget per platform and per evidence class. Critical evidence has an index budget of one hour and must be live-verified at query time. This failover runbook was indexed at version seven. The provider now reports version eight, so the runbook is marked stale, left out of the answer, and the receipt says why. An unknown state is never treated as fresh. On our public demo, an edit to a Confluence page reached the next answer about sixty seconds later, with no manual sync.

Groundedness is where we made our most deliberate design decision. The common approach is a second model that judges each claim: up to eight more sequential calls per answer, with a verdict that changes from run to run. We made the groundedness library model-free. One model call writes the answer, under a prompt that allows only the supplied evidence, copies numbers, dates and names exactly, ends every sentence with an evidence marker, and permits a single word, ABSTAIN. Pure Python then attaches each sentence to its evidence, and the same input produces the same grounding report, every time.

A lexical verifier scores every citation on content-token overlap, with negation cues for contradictions, and a numeric gate: a claim stating a number, a date or a time the evidence does not contain is never marked supported. Coverage below sixty percent, or any contradiction, means abstain. When the model adds unsupported claims, the pipeline keeps only the fully supported claims that address the question, re-verifies that subset, and labels the answer partial. No second model call is made, and quarantined injection text can never support a claim.

Every ask, decision, revocation and reveal is appended to an audit log. Each event hashes the previous hash, its sequence number and its payload, so a modified, deleted or reordered event is detectable, and the whole chain verifies in one call. Sam Lee works in compliance and sees who asked, which documents were candidates, each allow or deny with its rule, and the receipt. The answer text is withheld, because Sam cannot open the board deck. Sam enters a reason and reveals it, and the reveal is itself recorded in the chain.

Three pure Python libraries, access control, freshness and groundedness, depend on Pydantic alone and test without a network. A FastAPI service composes them, with Postgres and pgvector, Celery workers, a Next.js front end and an MCP server with eighteen tools, in one Docker Compose file. Generation runs on the Tencent Cloud ADP Chat API, and retrieval in the demo uses local deterministic vectors, so the whole demo runs on the free plan.

We wrote the architecture, the data model and the API contract before the code, so three people could build three libraries in parallel against shared interfaces and mock providers. Every library boots without secrets and tests offline. That is BrainSauce.
